assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Gas
items.clue: The state in which particles are far apart and move randomly.

items.label: Melting point
items.clue: The single temperature at which a substance both freezes and thaws.

items.label: Solid
items.clue: The state in which particles are packed closely in a fixed arrangement.

items.label: Liquid
items.clue: The state in which particles are close together but can move past one another.

questions.stem: At which temperature does a liquid change into a solid?

options.text: At its melting point, the same value as for melting
At its freezing point, a lower value than melting
At its boiling point, where condensing happens
At any temperature far below room warmth

questions.explanation: Melting and freezing both take place at the melting point.

questions.stem: Bromine vapour is cooled until it becomes a liquid. Which change of state is this, and at which temperature does it happen?

options.text: Condensing, at the condensing point of bromine
Condensing, at the boiling point of bromine
Freezing, at the melting point of bromine
Condensing, at bromine's melting point

questions.explanation: Boiling and condensing both take place at the boiling point.

questions.stem: In the simple model of the three states of matter, how are the particles represented?

options.text: As spheres drawn to the true size of an atom
As spheres that swell when the solid melts
As small solid spheres of the same kind
As tiny cubes stacked in a neat grid

questions.explanation: The specification states that in this model particles are represented by small solid spheres.

questions.stem: A solid is heated until it melts. Using the simple particle model, what happens to the particles?

options.text: They soften and change into smaller spheres
They break up into several smaller particles
They lose their shape and flow into each other
They stay the same but move further apart

questions.explanation: A change of state alters the arrangement and movement of the particles, not the particles themselves.

questions.stem: Substance X melts at 801 degrees C and substance Y melts at -7 degrees C. What does this tell you about the two substances?

options.text: The particles in X must be much heavier than in Y
The forces between the particles in X are much stronger
Substance Y has no forces between its particles
Y has stronger forces, so it melts much sooner

questions.explanation: The stronger the forces between the particles, the higher the melting point.

questions.stem: Why do some substances need much more energy to boil than others?

options.text: Because the particles they contain are larger and heavier
Because they have to be heated for a much longer time
Because the forces between their particles are stronger
Because a greater mass of substance is being used

questions.explanation: The energy needed to change state depends on the strength of the forces between the particles.

questions.stem: Ethanol melts at -114 degrees C and boils at 78 degrees C. What is the state of ethanol at 25 degrees C?

options.text: Gas, because 25 degrees C is above the melting point
Solid, because 25 degrees C is far below 78 degrees
Liquid, because 25 degrees C lies between the two values
Liquid and gas together in about equal amounts

questions.explanation: A substance is a liquid between its melting point and its boiling point.

questions.stem: Substance P has a melting point of -219 degrees C and a boiling point of -183 degrees C. What is the state of P at 20 degrees C?

options.text: Liquid, since 20 degrees C is above its melting point
Solid, because both quoted values are below zero
Liquid, which is normal at room temperature
Gas, since 20 degrees C is above its boiling point

questions.explanation: Above the boiling point the substance is a gas, whatever sign the quoted values carry.

questions.stem: Sodium chloride melts at 801 degrees C but chlorine melts at -101 degrees C. Which explanation of this difference is correct?

options.text: Sodium chloride has strong ionic attractions to break
The covalent bonds inside chlorine break easily as it melts
Chlorine has fewer bonds, so it melts a lot sooner
Sodium chloride particles are much heavier than chlorine

questions.explanation: Different bonding gives forces of very different strengths, so far more energy is needed to melt the ionic lattice.

questions.stem: A student says that one copper atom is shiny, can be bent and conducts electricity. Why is this wrong?

options.text: A single atom is shiny but it cannot conduct
Bulk properties belong to whole structures
Only atoms that are inside a compound gain them
An atom is too small to see, so nothing is known

questions.explanation: Properties such as shine, malleability and conductivity come from very many atoms arranged and bonded together.

questions.stem: (HT only) Which of these is a limitation of the simple model of the three states of matter?

options.text: The model draws far too few particles to be realistic
The model cannot explain any melting or boiling at all
The model shows solid, liquid and gas apart
The model shows no forces between the particles

questions.explanation: The specification lists the absence of forces as one of the limitations of the simple model.

questions.stem: (HT only) In the simple model the particles are solid inelastic spheres with no forces between them. Why does this make boiling hard to explain?

options.text: Boiling overcomes forces the model leaves out
The spheres are drawn much larger than real atoms
The model uses far fewer particles than a real sample
The particles in the model move much too slowly

questions.explanation: Energy is needed at the boiling point to overcome forces between particles, and the model contains no forces.
